PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 149 — Lesson 173: Gastrointestinal, Hepatic & Nutritional Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Integrate abdominal symptoms, gastrointestinal bleeding, luminal disease, hepatobiliary and pancreatic disorders, liver dysfunction, nutrition, medications, and life-stage risk to identify emergencies, build a focused differential, select useful testing, begin safe care, and close the follow-up loop.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize the unstable abdomen, major GI bleeding, obstruction, perforation, mesenteric ischemia, ascending cholangitis, severe pancreatitis, acute liver failure, and cirrhosis-related emergencies.
  • Build a differential from symptom location, time course, bowel pattern, bleeding pattern, exposures, medications, surgery, pregnancy potential, and comorbidity.
  • Interpret CBC, chemistry, lipase, liver tests, bilirubin, albumin, INR, stool studies, and imaging as parts of a clinical pattern rather than isolated results.
  • Distinguish common outpatient syndromes from alarm-feature presentations that require endoscopy, imaging, specialty evaluation, or emergency care.
  • Apply evidence-based principles to GERD, dyspepsia and H. pylori, diarrhea, constipation, inflammatory bowel disease, gallbladder disease, pancreatitis, MASLD, and cirrhosis.
  • Use nutrition, medication safety, shared decisions, explicit return precautions, and result ownership to complete the plan.

Part 1 — The FNP Integration Task

Abdominal symptoms are common, but the same symptom can represent benign, chronic, inflammatory, obstructive, ischemic, infectious, malignant, or extra-abdominal disease. “Abdominal pain” is not a diagnosis. The FNP must first determine physiologic stability, then convert the history and examination into an anatomically and mechanistically coherent problem representation.

Use the ABDOMEN framework:

  • A — Assess acuity and stability: vital signs, perfusion, mental status, bleeding, hydration, respiratory effort, and severe pain.
  • B — Build the pattern: location, radiation, onset, triggers, meals, stool, emesis, urinary and gynecologic symptoms, exposures, medications, surgery, and risk factors.
  • D — Decide the dangerous alternatives: bleeding, perforation, obstruction, ischemia, infection, torsion, ectopic pregnancy, acute hepatobiliary disease, and toxic-metabolic illness.
  • O — Order focused tests: each laboratory, image, or procedure must answer a question and change management.
  • M — Manage the likely syndrome: stabilize, stop aggravating exposures, provide evidence-aligned care, and avoid unsafe empiricism.
  • E — Escalate when necessary: emergency transfer, urgent imaging, endoscopy, surgery, gastroenterology, hepatology, or nutrition support.
  • N — Navigate follow-up: own pending results, verify response, confirm eradication or healing when indicated, and provide return precautions.

Part 2 — First Decision: Stable or Unstable?

Before deciding whether pain is epigastric, biliary, or intestinal, assess whether the patient can safely remain in the outpatient setting. Concerning findings include hypotension, syncope, confusion, hypoxemia, active hematemesis or large-volume hematochezia, rigid abdomen, rebound or involuntary guarding, rapidly increasing distention, severe pain out of proportion to the examination, persistent bilious or feculent vomiting, inability to maintain hydration, or evidence of sepsis.

Normal vital signs do not completely exclude dangerous disease, particularly in older adults, immunocompromised patients, pregnant patients, and people taking beta blockers. Repeat the examination when the story and the initial findings do not agree.

Part 3 — Build a High-Value Abdominal History

Characterize onset, location, migration, radiation, severity, progression, relation to meals or defecation, vomiting, stool frequency and appearance, fever, weight change, jaundice, pruritus, urinary symptoms, vaginal bleeding, and pregnancy possibility. Ask about travel, sick contacts, food and water exposure, antibiotics, alcohol, cannabis, prior abdominal surgery, gallstones, pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, liver disease, and family history of GI cancer.

Medication review is diagnostic. NSAIDs can contribute to ulcer disease and bleeding; antibiotics can precede C. difficile; opioids and anticholinergics worsen constipation; anticoagulants amplify bleeding; GLP-1 receptor agonists can affect GI symptoms; and supplements may cause hepatotoxicity. The question is not merely “What do you take?” but “Could a medicine produce, worsen, or conceal this pattern?”

Part 4 — Location Helps, but Does Not Diagnose

  • Right upper quadrant: biliary disease, hepatitis, hepatic congestion, lower-lobe pneumonia, or referred pain.
  • Epigastric: GERD, gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, pancreatitis, biliary disease, myocardial ischemia, or aortic disease.
  • Right lower quadrant: appendicitis, ileitis, ovarian pathology, ectopic pregnancy, ureteral stone, or hernia.
  • Left lower quadrant: diverticular disease, colitis, constipation, ovarian pathology, or urinary disease.
  • Diffuse pain: gastroenteritis, obstruction, metabolic disease, peritonitis, ischemia, medication effects, or functional disorders.

Radiation and evolution refine the pattern. Pain migrating from the periumbilical region to the right lower quadrant supports appendiceal irritation; epigastric pain radiating to the back may suggest pancreatic disease; shoulder pain can reflect diaphragmatic irritation. None of these findings is independently definitive.

Part 5 — The Acute Abdomen

An acute abdomen is a clinical syndrome suggesting urgent intra-abdominal pathology, not a single disease. Peritoneal inflammation can produce involuntary guarding, rebound, pain with movement, and a patient who prefers to remain still. Obstruction can cause colicky pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation; late disease may become constant and toxic. Mesenteric ischemia may initially cause severe pain disproportionate to limited examination findings.

Do not delay escalation while pursuing a perfect outpatient diagnosis. Stabilization, pregnancy testing when relevant, appropriate laboratory assessment, and timely imaging or surgical evaluation take priority.

Part 6 — GI Bleeding: Describe the Source and the Physiology

Hematemesis and melena often suggest an upper GI source. Hematochezia commonly reflects lower GI bleeding, but brisk upper bleeding can also present this way. Dark stool from iron or bismuth is not equivalent to melena; the full history and examination matter.

Assess hemodynamics, orthostatic symptoms, mental status, perfusion, medication exposure, liver disease, prior ulcer or varices, and comorbid cardiovascular disease. An initial hemoglobin can underestimate acute blood loss because plasma and red-cell loss occur together. Active bleeding with instability requires emergency evaluation and resuscitation, not routine outpatient testing.

Part 7 — Occult Blood Loss and Iron Deficiency

Chronic GI blood loss may present as fatigue, exertional dyspnea, pica, microcytosis, or iron deficiency rather than visible bleeding. Iron deficiency in an adult is a mechanism to explain, not simply a number to replace. Menstrual loss, diet, malabsorption, medications, and GI sources must be considered in context.

A negative office stool test does not safely close the evaluation when the patient has iron-deficiency anemia or alarm features. Determine the appropriate GI and gynecologic evaluation, urgency, and follow-up based on age, symptoms, history, and risk.

Part 8 — Dysphagia and Odynophagia

First distinguish oropharyngeal dysphagia—difficulty initiating a swallow, coughing, choking, nasal regurgitation—from esophageal dysphagia—food sticking after swallowing. Solids progressing to liquids raises concern for mechanical narrowing; difficulty with solids and liquids may indicate a motility disorder, although patterns overlap.

Progressive dysphagia, odynophagia, food impaction, weight loss, bleeding, anemia, or aspiration risk requires prompt evaluation. A patient unable to handle secretions or with an obstructing food bolus needs emergency care. Do not repeatedly label dysphagia as uncomplicated reflux.

Part 9 — GERD: Symptoms, Alarm Features, and Competing Diagnoses

Typical GERD symptoms include heartburn and regurgitation, but chest discomfort demands appropriate cardiac risk assessment. Alarm features such as dysphagia, GI bleeding, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, or anemia change the pathway and may warrant endoscopic evaluation rather than indefinite empiric treatment.

Management integrates lifestyle triggers that matter to the individual, appropriate acid suppression, correct medication timing, and reassessment. Persistent symptoms require a diagnostic reset: confirm adherence and diagnosis, consider medication effects and alternative disorders, and determine whether specialty testing is needed.

Part 10 — Dyspepsia, H. pylori, and Test-of-Cure

Dyspepsia may include epigastric pain, burning, early satiety, or postprandial fullness. Age, gastric-cancer risk, NSAID use, family history, and alarm features determine whether noninvasive H. pylori testing, endoscopy, or another strategy is appropriate.

Current ACG guidance emphasizes treating confirmed H. pylori infection and documenting eradication. Breath or stool antigen testing assesses active infection more reliably than serology in many settings. Test-of-cure is performed after treatment at an appropriate interval, with acid suppression, bismuth, and antibiotics held as directed to reduce false-negative results. Antibiotic selection must account for prior exposure, allergy, local resistance, and current guidance; do not automatically use clarithromycin-containing therapy when susceptibility is unknown.

Part 11 — Peptic Ulcer Disease and NSAID Risk

H. pylori and NSAID exposure are major ulcer mechanisms. Risk rises with older age, prior ulcer or bleeding, higher NSAID dose, corticosteroid or antithrombotic combinations, and serious comorbidity. Ask about over-the-counter ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, and combination products.

Complications include bleeding, perforation, penetration, and gastric outlet obstruction. Sudden severe pain with rigidity suggests perforation; recurrent vomiting and early satiety may suggest obstruction. Treatment must address the cause, not only suppress acid.

Part 12 — Nausea and Vomiting

Organize causes into GI obstruction or inflammation, neurologic disease, pregnancy, endocrine-metabolic disease, medication or toxin effects, infection, vestibular disease, and functional syndromes. Characterize emesis, timing, abdominal distention, bowel output, headache or neurologic signs, cannabis exposure, pregnancy potential, and hydration.

Bilious vomiting, hematemesis, feculent emesis, severe headache with neurologic findings, peritoneal signs, significant electrolyte disturbance, or inability to maintain fluids requires escalation. Antiemetics can relieve symptoms but should not conceal an unaddressed surgical or metabolic process.

Part 13 — Acute Diarrhea

Most uncomplicated acute watery diarrhea is self-limited. Priorities are hydration, severity assessment, exposure history, and selective testing. Fever, blood, severe abdominal pain, sepsis, immunocompromise, recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure, travel, outbreak risk, or prolonged symptoms change the evaluation.

Avoid reflex antibiotic prescribing. Some infections require targeted treatment, while unnecessary antibiotics can cause adverse effects, resistance, or worsen selected toxin-mediated illness. Antimotility therapy is not appropriate for every patient, especially when invasive infection or toxic colitis is suspected.

Part 14 — Chronic Diarrhea and Malabsorption

Classify chronic diarrhea as watery, fatty, or inflammatory while considering overlap. Review diet, medications, surgery, travel, immune status, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, anemia, blood, and family history. Differential diagnosis includes celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, microscopic colitis, pancreatic insufficiency, bile-acid diarrhea, endocrine disease, chronic infection, and medication effects.

Do not diagnose IBS solely because basic tests are normal. Nocturnal diarrhea, bleeding, weight loss, fever, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, onset later in life, or a family history of IBD or GI cancer demands broader evaluation.

Part 15 — Constipation and Obstruction Safety

Assess stool frequency and form, straining, incomplete evacuation, medication burden, hydration, mobility, neurologic disease, pelvic-floor symptoms, and secondary causes. Alarm features include new or progressive symptoms with bleeding, anemia, weight loss, severe pain, vomiting, fever, a mass, or a strong cancer history.

Acute distention, pain, vomiting, and failure to pass stool or flatus raise concern for obstruction or ileus. Before escalating laxatives, determine whether the bowel is safely patent and whether fecal impaction or urinary retention is present.

Part 16 — IBS Is a Positive Clinical Diagnosis

Irritable bowel syndrome is characterized by recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and altered stool pattern without identified structural disease explaining the syndrome. A positive diagnosis uses a compatible pattern and limited targeted evaluation rather than endless exclusion.

Management may include dietary strategy, fiber selection, symptom-directed therapy, sleep, stress and gut-brain interventions, and a therapeutic alliance. New alarm features require reassessment; a prior IBS label must never prevent evaluation of a new organic process.

Part 17 — Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease can produce chronic diarrhea, blood, urgency, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia, and extraintestinal manifestations. Crohn disease can affect any GI segment and may cause strictures, fistulas, or perianal disease; ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and begins in the rectum with continuous involvement.

Severe bloody diarrhea, fever, tachycardia, distention, dehydration, or systemic toxicity may represent severe colitis or toxic megacolon and requires urgent care. FNP responsibilities include recognition, infection assessment, medication and vaccination safety, nutrition, cancer-surveillance coordination, and timely gastroenterology partnership.

Part 18 — Diverticular Disease

Diverticulosis is common and often asymptomatic. Diverticulitis typically causes focal lower abdominal pain, often left-sided, with tenderness and sometimes fever or bowel change. Differential diagnosis includes colitis, malignancy, urinary disease, and gynecologic pathology.

Disposition depends on diagnostic confidence, severity, oral intake, immune status, comorbidity, and concern for abscess, perforation, obstruction, or fistula. Antibiotics are not automatically required for every uncomplicated immunocompetent patient; use current guidance and individualized risk. Peritoneal signs, sepsis, uncontrolled pain, or inability to hydrate requires escalation.

Part 19 — Appendicitis Across the Lifespan

Appendicitis may begin with vague periumbilical discomfort and migrate to the right lower quadrant, but classic features are not universal. Older adults and pregnant patients can present atypically; children may deteriorate rapidly. Anorexia, nausea, fever, focal tenderness, and pain with movement can support the diagnosis.

Risk scores may organize thinking but do not replace clinical judgment. Pregnancy testing, urinalysis, laboratory tests, and age-appropriate imaging help address competing diagnoses. Persistent focal pain or peritoneal findings require urgent surgical evaluation.

Part 20 — Gallstones and Acute Cholecystitis

Biliary colic typically causes episodic right upper quadrant or epigastric pain after gallbladder contraction without sustained inflammation. Prolonged pain, fever, focal tenderness, leukocytosis, or a positive Murphy-type finding increases concern for acute cholecystitis.

Right upper quadrant ultrasonography is usually the initial imaging test for suspected gallbladder disease. Liver tests and lipase help evaluate ductal obstruction or pancreatitis. Pain that resolves does not eliminate the need for follow-up when symptomatic gallstones are suspected.

Part 21 — Ascending Cholangitis Is an Emergency

Biliary obstruction with infection can cause fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice; hypotension and altered mental status indicate severe disease. Patients may not display the complete classic pattern.

Suspected cholangitis requires emergency evaluation, antimicrobial therapy, supportive care, and urgent biliary drainage coordination. Outpatient oral antibiotics alone do not relieve an obstructed infected biliary system.

Part 22 — Acute Pancreatitis

Acute pancreatitis commonly presents with persistent severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back, with nausea and vomiting. Gallstones and alcohol are major causes, but medications, hypertriglyceridemia, procedures, and other etiologies matter.

Diagnosis generally requires two of three features: characteristic pain, pancreatic enzymes more than three times the upper limit of normal, or compatible imaging. Imaging is not automatically needed to prove every clear case. Assess volume status, respiratory and renal function, systemic inflammatory response, biliary obstruction, and ability to tolerate oral intake. Hypotension, hypoxemia, acute kidney injury, altered mental status, or organ failure indicates high-risk disease.

Part 23 — Interpreting Liver Tests by Pattern

AST and ALT primarily signal hepatocellular injury; alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin help identify cholestatic or obstructive patterns. Albumin and INR contribute information about hepatic synthetic function, although both have nonhepatic influences. The magnitude of enzyme elevation does not directly equal remaining liver function.

Use the pattern, trajectory, symptoms, medication and supplement history, alcohol exposure, metabolic risk, viral risk, pregnancy status, and imaging together. A normal aminotransferase value does not exclude clinically significant chronic liver disease.

Part 24 — Jaundice: Production, Processing, or Flow

Organize hyperbilirubinemia into increased production, impaired hepatic uptake or conjugation, hepatocellular dysfunction, and impaired bile flow. Examine urine and stool color, pruritus, pain, fever, weight loss, medication exposure, hemolysis clues, and liver-disease signs.

Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain suggests cholangitis; painless progressive jaundice with weight loss raises concern for malignancy or obstruction; jaundice with coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, or encephalopathy may indicate acute liver failure. These pathways require urgent escalation.

Part 25 — Viral Hepatitis and Prevention

Risk assessment includes birth cohort and current screening recommendations, country of origin, household or sexual exposure, injection or intranasal drug use, tattoos or procedures in unsafe settings, occupational exposure, and immunization history. Symptoms can be absent even when chronic injury is present.

Interpret antigen, antibody, and nucleic-acid tests as a pattern. Provide hepatitis A and B immunization when indicated, harm-reduction counseling, pregnancy-specific coordination, and linkage to treatment. A positive screening test is not closed until confirmatory testing, counseling, staging, and referral or treatment have occurred.

Part 26 — MASLD: Metabolic Risk and Fibrosis Risk

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is linked to obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular risk. The clinically important question is not only whether steatosis is present, but whether significant fibrosis may be developing.

Evaluate alcohol exposure and competing liver disease, address cardiometabolic risk, and use validated noninvasive fibrosis assessment when appropriate. Aminotransferases alone cannot reliably exclude advanced fibrosis. Patients with concerning fibrosis risk, diagnostic uncertainty, or signs of advanced disease need hepatology evaluation.

Part 27 — Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease and Medication Injury

Use nonjudgmental, quantified alcohol assessment and screen for alcohol use disorder. Sudden cessation can cause dangerous withdrawal; treatment planning must account for severity and safety. Alcohol-related injury can coexist with viral, metabolic, or medication-related disease.

Drug-induced liver injury requires a complete prescription, over-the-counter, supplement, and timing history. Stop suspected harmful exposures when clinically appropriate and evaluate alternative causes. Marked injury with jaundice, rising INR, hypoglycemia, or altered mental status demands urgent specialist or emergency assessment.

Part 28 — Compensated vs Decompensated Cirrhosis

Compensated cirrhosis may be clinically subtle. Decompensation is marked by ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, or related complications. Examine for muscle wasting, jaundice, spider angiomas, edema, ascites, splenomegaly, and cognitive change, but absence of classic signs does not exclude disease.

Care includes cause-directed treatment, medication review, nutrition, vaccination, variceal and liver-cancer surveillance coordination, renal protection, and early hepatology partnership. NSAIDs, sedatives, dehydration, infection, constipation, and nephrotoxic exposures can precipitate deterioration.

Part 29 — Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

New or worsening ascites requires evaluation of cause and complications. In cirrhosis, fever, abdominal pain, tenderness, encephalopathy, hypotension, leukocytosis, or acute kidney injury may signal spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, but presentation can be subtle or asymptomatic.

Diagnostic paracentesis is central when SBP is suspected and for many nonelective admissions with cirrhosis and ascites. Do not postpone urgent evaluation because the abdomen is not very tender. Ascites also marks hepatic decompensation and should prompt specialist and transplant-evaluation consideration when appropriate.

Part 30 — Hepatic Encephalopathy

Hepatic encephalopathy ranges from subtle cognitive change to somnolence or coma. Search for precipitating factors: infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration, renal dysfunction, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, and medication nonadherence.

Ammonia level alone neither confirms nor safely excludes the diagnosis. Altered mental status still requires assessment for stroke, hypoglycemia, intoxication, sepsis, medication effect, and other causes. New or severe encephalopathy is not routine outpatient confusion.

Part 31 — Nutrition Is a Clinical Vital Sign

Assess weight trajectory, intake, food access, dentition, swallowing, nausea, stool pattern, restrictive diets, substance use, depression, function, and disease-related catabolism. BMI alone can miss sarcopenia or malnutrition, especially when edema or ascites masks tissue loss.

Unintentional weight loss, muscle wasting, hypoalbuminemia in context, micronutrient risk, and functional decline require cause-directed evaluation. Nutrition referral is treatment, not an afterthought. In severe undernutrition, recognize refeeding risk and coordinate cautious nutritional rehabilitation.

Part 32 — Life-Stage Modifiers

Children: age-specific dehydration signs, bilious emesis, intussusception, appendicitis, and ingestion risk require a low threshold for escalation. Pregnancy: consider ectopic pregnancy, hyperemesis, hypertensive liver disease, gallbladder disease, and pregnancy-specific imaging and medication safety. Older adults: serious disease may present with muted pain or fever; medication effects, ischemia, malignancy, dehydration, and atypical appendicitis deserve attention.

Immunocompromised patients may lack expected inflammatory signs. Adapt the threshold for imaging, consultation, and emergency referral to the patient's physiology and ability to compensate—not to age alone.

Part 33 — Board-Style Case 1: GI Bleeding

A 69-year-old taking naproxen and apixaban reports black tarry stools, weakness, and near-syncope. BP is 88/54 mm Hg and HR is 118/min.

Reasoning: Melena plus shock physiology suggests major GI bleeding. The priority is emergency transfer and resuscitative evaluation, not an office fecal occult blood test or routine PPI follow-up. Medication history explains bleeding amplification but does not reduce urgency.

Part 34 — Board-Style Case 2: Biliary Sepsis

A 74-year-old has fever, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, confusion, and hypotension.

Reasoning: This pattern suggests severe ascending cholangitis with sepsis. The patient needs emergency stabilization, antimicrobials, and urgent biliary drainage coordination. Waiting for outpatient ultrasonography is unsafe.

Part 35 — Board-Style Case 3: Acute Pancreatitis

A 48-year-old has persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting, and lipase five times the upper limit of normal. Oxygen saturation is 89%, creatinine is rising, and BP is falling.

Reasoning: Characteristic pain plus markedly elevated lipase supports acute pancreatitis. Hypoxemia, kidney injury, and hypotension indicate organ dysfunction and high-risk disease requiring urgent hospital care.

Part 36 — Board-Style Case 4: Cirrhosis With New Confusion

A patient with cirrhosis and ascites develops confusion, abdominal discomfort, and acute kidney injury without high fever.

Reasoning: Do not assume uncomplicated hepatic encephalopathy. SBP may be subtle and can precipitate encephalopathy and renal dysfunction. The patient needs urgent evaluation, diagnostic paracentesis, and assessment for other precipitants.

Part 37 — Board-Style Case 5: Dysphagia and Weight Loss

A 63-year-old reports progressively worsening solid-food dysphagia, then difficulty with liquids, iron-deficiency anemia, and 8-kg unintentional weight loss.

Reasoning: Progressive dysphagia, anemia, and weight loss are alarm features for mechanical obstruction or malignancy. Repeated empiric reflux treatment is not sufficient; prompt endoscopic evaluation and safe nutrition planning are required.

Part 38 — Common Board Traps

  • Trap: A normal first hemoglobin excludes serious acute bleeding. Correction: early hemoglobin may not reflect total acute loss; physiology and ongoing bleeding drive urgency.
  • Trap: All epigastric pain is GERD. Correction: consider ACS, pancreatitis, biliary disease, ulcer complication, and aortic pathology.
  • Trap: Every diverticulitis case needs antibiotics. Correction: severity, complications, immune status, and current guidance determine therapy.
  • Trap: Normal AST and ALT exclude advanced chronic liver disease. Correction: fibrosis risk and synthetic/portal features matter.
  • Trap: Elevated ammonia proves hepatic encephalopathy. Correction: diagnosis is clinical and competing causes must be assessed.
  • Trap: A symptom-control prescription closes the visit. Correction: disposition, pending-result ownership, response assessment, and safety-netting are part of treatment.

Part 39 — The Final Board-Ready Algorithm

  1. Stabilize first: identify shock, bleeding, peritonitis, obstruction, sepsis, dehydration, respiratory compromise, or altered mental status.
  2. Represent the problem: patient context + time course + location + key associated features + risks.
  3. Name the cannot-miss diagnoses: choose threats that match the anatomy and physiology.
  4. Select discriminating tests: know what each result would change; avoid indiscriminate panels.
  5. Treat cause and physiology: hydration, bleeding risk, medication exposures, infection, obstruction, inflammation, and nutrition.
  6. Choose disposition: outpatient, expedited specialty care, urgent imaging/procedure, or emergency transfer.
  7. Close the loop: specify who reviews results, when reassessment occurs, what response is expected, and which symptoms require immediate care.

High-Yield Summary

  • Stability and peritoneal or bleeding signs outrank a precise outpatient label.
  • Hematemesis and melena suggest upper bleeding; brisk upper bleeding can produce hematochezia.
  • Dysphagia, bleeding, anemia, weight loss, persistent vomiting, or progressive symptoms are alarm features.
  • Confirmed H. pylori infection requires treatment and documented eradication.
  • Bloody diarrhea with toxicity, severe colitis, obstruction, cholangitis, and organ-failing pancreatitis require urgent care.
  • Liver-test patterns describe injury; INR, albumin, clinical decompensation, and portal complications help assess function and severity.
  • Ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy mark cirrhosis decompensation.
  • Nutrition, medication safety, specialist coordination, and result ownership are core FNP responsibilities.

Clinical note: This lesson is educational and emphasizes reasoning principles. Apply current guidelines, local protocols, patient-specific factors, and collaborative or emergency resources in practice.
